claim: Glucocorticoid (GC) variation has long been thought to reflect variation in organismal 'stress'
source: Glucocorticoid (GC) variation has long been thought to reflect variation in organismal 'stress,' but associations between GCs and Darwinian fitness components are diverse in magnitude, direction, and highly context-dependent.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical interpretation of GC variation in the scientific literature, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: Associations between GCs and Darwinian fitness components are diverse in magnitude, direction, and highly context-dependent
source: Glucocorticoid (GC) variation has long been thought to reflect variation in organismal 'stress,' but associations between GCs and Darwinian fitness components are diverse in magnitude, direction, and highly context-dependent.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to the literature on GC-fitness relationships, as elaborated in later citations.

claim: GCs orchestrate energy availability to anticipate and recover from predictable and unpredictable environmental fluctuations and challenges
source: Amongst an array of effects in many physiological systems, GCs orchestrate energy availability to anticipate and recover from predictable and unpredictable environmental fluctuations and challenges.
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanistic role of GCs, drawing from established physiological knowledge.

claim: An increase in metabolic rate was associated with an increase in GC levels in 20 out of 21 studies
source: We found that an increase in metabolic rate was associated with an increase in GC levels in 20 out of 21 studies (32 out of 35 effect sizes).
evidence: This is a direct report of the meta-analysis results, supported by the data collected from the reviewed studies.

claim: An increase in metabolic rate was associated with an increase in GC levels in 32 out of 35 effect sizes
source: We found that an increase in metabolic rate was associated with an increase in GC levels in 20 out of 21 studies (32 out of 35 effect sizes).
evidence: This is a direct report of the meta-analysis results, supported by the data collected from the reviewed studies.

claim: There was a strong positive correlation between the increases in metabolic rate and GCs (p=0.003)
source: More importantly, there was a strong positive correlation between the increases in metabolic rate and GCs (p=0.003).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the meta-regression analysis, supported by the quantitative data analysis.

claim: The pattern of association between metabolic rate and GCs was similar in birds and mammals
source: This pattern was similar in birds and mammals, and independent of the nature of the experimental treatment.
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis showing no significant difference between taxa.

claim: The pattern of association between metabolic rate and GCs was independent of the nature of the experimental treatment
source: This pattern was similar in birds and mammals, and independent of the nature of the experimental treatment.
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis showing no significant effect of treatment type.

claim: Metabolic rate is a major driver of GC variation within individuals
source: We conclude that metabolic rate is a major driver of GC variation within individuals.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the meta-analysis results showing strong correlation between MR and GC changes.

claim: Glucocorticoid hormones were identified by Hans Selye (1907–1982) as the key molecular mediators of the 'stress reaction'
source: Glucocorticoid hormones (GCs; e.g. cortisol, corticosterone) were identified by Hans Selye (1907–1982) as the key molecular mediators of the 'stress reaction' and named in reference to their capacity to increase glucose in blood.
evidence: This is a historical fact about the discovery and naming of glucocorticoids, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Glucocorticoids were named in reference to their capacity to increase glucose in blood
source: Glucocorticoid hormones (GCs; e.g. cortisol, corticosterone) were identified by Hans Selye (1907–1982) as the key molecular mediators of the 'stress reaction' and named in reference to their capacity to increase glucose in blood.
evidence: This is a historical fact about the naming of glucocorticoids, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Selye highlighted the fundamental role of GCs in the 'general adaptation syndrome'
source: Selye highlighted the fundamental role of GCs in the 'general adaptation syndrome,' that is, 'the physiological mechanisms that help to raise resistance to damage as such, irrespective of the specific nature of the damaging agents' (Selye, 1950).
evidence: This is supported by a direct citation to Selye's 1950 work.

claim: Selye's definition of stress was 'the nonspecific response of the body on any demand on it'
source: Indeed, towards the later stages of his career, Selye's definition of stress was 'the nonspecific response of the body on any demand on it' (Selye, 1976), making the point that very different stimuli (i.e. 'stressors') triggered the same response.
evidence: This is supported by a direct citation to Selye's 1976 work.

claim: In the literature, the perspective on 'stress' and GCs has changed over time, with GCs being widely linked to negative outcomes
source: However, in the literature this perspective has changed over time, and 'stress' and, by extension, GCs have been widely linked to negative outcomes (but see Koolhaas et al., 2011; Herman, 2022; MacDougall-Shackleton et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about trends in the scientific literature, supported by citations to works that challenge this view.

claim: GCs have predominated over other traits throughout the stress physiology literature
source: Indeed, GCs have predominated over other traits throughout the stress physiology literature, to the point of being referred to as vertebrate 'stress hormones' (Madliger et al., 2015; Madliger and Love, 2014; McCormick and Romero, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple papers discussing the prevalence of GC research.

claim: Several authors have argued against the simplified view of GC regulation during the past decades
source: While several authors have argued against this simplified view of GC regulation during the past decades (e.g. Koolhaas et al., 2011; MacDougall-Shackleton et al., 2019; Herman, 2022; Romero, 2004; Landys et al., 2006; Bonier et al., 2009), such association prevails, in the sense that publications still abound in which GC levels are assumed to provide information on organismal stress.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to papers that have challenged the simplified view of GCs as stress hormones.

claim: Acute increases in circulating GCs are a defining aspect of the so-called 'stress response'
source: Furthermore, acute increases in circulating GCs are a defining aspect of the so-called 'stress response' (Koolhaas et al., 2011; Sapolsky et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established works on stress physiology.

claim: Higher GC levels have traditionally been interpreted as an indication of homeostatic unbalance, poor condition, implicating low fitness prospects
source: Consequently, higher GC levels circulating in plasma or deposited in keratinized tissues (i.e. hair or feathers) have traditionally been interpreted as an indication of homeostatic unbalance, poor condition, implicating low fitness prospects (reviewed in Schoenle et al., 2021; Romero and Fairhurst, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review papers on the traditional interpretation of GC levels.

claim: Associations between GCs and fitness (survival/reproduction) are diverse in direction and often nonexistent
source: However, the latter assumption is at best poorly supported by the literature, with associations between GCs and fitness (survival/reproduction) being diverse in direction and often nonexistent (Schoenle et al., 2021; Zimmer et al., 2022; Busch and Hayward, 2009; Bonier et al., 2009; Petrullo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies and reviews examining GC-fitness relationships.

claim: Sexual activity induces a GC increase in humans, horses, and rodents
source: The urgency of this question is further underlined by the observation that GCs also increase in response to experiences we would not normally qualify as stress; for example, sexual activity induces a GC increase in humans, horses, and rodents (Siciliani, 2000; Colborn et al., 1991; Buwalda et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing GC increases during sexual activity.

claim: Activation of the hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis represents a primary hormonal response to homeostatic challenges
source: Activation of the hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis represents a primary hormonal response to homeostatic challenges that, through the release of GCs, mobilizes the resources needed to fuel the current or anticipated rise in energy expenditure (current and anticipatory responses) or recover from an immediate threat that induced an unanticipated increase in energy expenditure (reactive response) (Herman et al., 2016; McEwen and Wingfield, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established works on HPA axis function.

claim: GCs are involved in the metabolism of most types of energy reserves, modulating glucose, fat, and protein metabolism in liver, skeletal muscle, and other target tissues
source: In this context, GCs are involved in the metabolism of most types of energy reserves, modulating glucose, fat, and protein metabolism in liver, skeletal muscle, and other target tissues (Box 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the metabolic role of GCs, drawing from established physiological knowledge and referenced to Box 1.

claim: The extent to which GC variation can be quantitatively explained as facilitator of variation in energy expenditure has rarely been addressed
source: Allusions to the energetic role of GCs and their tight link to energy expenditure are common in physiological and ecological studies, especially those using approaches which underline the adaptive function of GC responses (McEwen and Wingfield, 2003; Landys et al., 2006; Romero et al., 2009; Deviche et al., 2017), but the extent to which GC variation can be quantitatively explained as facilitator of variation in energy expenditure has rarely been addressed (but see Jimeno et al., 2018; Malkoc et al., 2021 supplementary information).
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in the literature, supported by citations to the few studies that have addressed this question.

claim: The treatment effect size on MR was on average 1.85 ± 0.87
source: Among the studies selected for inclusion in the analysis, the treatment effect size on MR was on average 1.85 ± 0.87 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the meta-analysis results, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Effects on GCs were positive in the majority of cases (32/35)
source: In accordance with prediction, effects on GCs were positive in the majority of cases (32/35; Figure 1), and consequently the overall average effect size deviated significantly from zero, with the average GC effect size estimated at 0.73 ± 0.11 (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the meta-analysis results, supported by data shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: The overall average GC effect size deviated significantly from zero, with the average GC effect size estimated at 0.73 ± 0.11
source: In accordance with prediction, effects on GCs were positive in the majority of cases (32/35; Figure 1), and consequently the overall average effect size deviated significantly from zero, with the average GC effect size estimated at 0.73 ± 0.11 (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the meta-analysis results, supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: The residual heterogeneity did not exceed the level expected by chance
source: It is further worth noting that the residual heterogeneity did not exceed the level expected by chance (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the meta-analysis, supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: MR Cohen's D was ln-transformed to normalize the distribution
source: MR Cohen's D was ln-transformed (see 'Materials and methods') to normalize the distribution (Figure 2), and AICc of models including ln MR were significantly lower compared to models including untransformed MR Cohen's D (AICc = 70.58 vs. 74.97, respectively).
evidence: This is a methodological decision supported by model comparison statistics.

claim: AICc of models including ln MR were significantly lower compared to models including untransformed MR Cohen's D (AICc = 70.58 vs. 74.97, respectively)
source: MR Cohen's D was ln-transformed (see 'Materials and methods') to normalize the distribution (Figure 2), and AICc of models including ln MR were significantly lower compared to models including untransformed MR Cohen's D (AICc = 70.58 vs. 74.97, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from model comparison, supporting the use of ln-transformed MR.

claim: The association between MR and GC effect sizes remained statistically significant when adding taxa, before/after, experiment/control effect, metabolic variable, or treatment type one by one to the model
source: The association between MR and GC effect sizes remained statistically significant when adding taxa, before/after, experiment/control effect, metabolic variable, or treatment type one by one to the model.
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-regression analysis testing the robustness of the main effect.

claim: None of the variables (taxa, before/after, experiment/control effect, metabolic variable, or treatment type) had a significant effect on GC effect size
source: Furthermore, none of these variables had a significant effect on GC effect size, nor did the association between MR and GC effect sizes depend on those factors (i.e. interactions between these variables and MR effect sizes were always nonsignificant; Table 2, Supplementary file 4, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-regression analysis, supported by data shown in Table 2 and supplementary materials.

claim: The association between MR and GC effect sizes did not depend on taxa, before/after, experiment/control effect, metabolic variable, or treatment type
source: Furthermore, none of these variables had a significant effect on GC effect size, nor did the association between MR and GC effect sizes depend on those factors (i.e. interactions between these variables and MR effect sizes were always nonsignificant; Table 2, Supplementary file 4, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-regression analysis testing for interaction effects.

claim: Studies including within-individual variation (i.e. experiment/control effect) reported higher GC effect sizes
source: Despite these modulators being nonsignificant, the associations were in the expected directions, with studies including within-individual variation (i.e. experiment/control effect), and not including a before/after effect reporting higher GC effect sizes (table in Supplementary file 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-regression analysis, supported by data shown in supplementary materials.

claim: Studies not including a before/after effect reported higher GC effect sizes
source: Despite these modulators being nonsignificant, the associations were in the expected directions, with studies including within-individual variation (i.e. experiment/control effect), and not including a before/after effect reporting higher GC effect sizes (table in Supplementary file 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-regression analysis, supported by data shown in supplementary materials.

claim: GC secretion facilitated increases in MR
source: The analysis confirmed our predictions, showing that experimental manipulations that increased MR induced a proportional increase in GCs (Figure 2), and our interpretation of this effect is that GC secretion facilitated increases in MR.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the meta-analysis results, based on the observed correlation between MR and GC changes.

claim: Fluctuations in energy turnover are a key factor driving variation in GC levels
source: This association indicates that fluctuations in energy turnover are a key factor driving variation in GC levels.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the meta-analysis results showing strong correlation between MR and GC changes.

claim: Downstream effects of GCs may be interpreted as allocation adjustments to the metabolic level at which organisms operate
source: From this perspective, the many downstream effects of GCs (e.g. downregulation of immune function and reproduction; McEwen and Wingfield, 2003; Sapolsky et al., 2000) may be interpreted as allocation adjustments to the metabolic level at which organisms operate.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the meta-analysis findings and cited literature on GC effects.

claim: Within-individual blood GC variation signals the MR at which the organism is functioning to all systems in the body
source: Specifically, within-individual blood GC variation signals the MR at which the organism is functioning to all systems in the body.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the meta-analysis findings about the MR-GC relationship.

claim: Downstream effects of GCs can be interpreted as evolved responses to MR fluctuations, reallocating resources in the face of shifting demands on the whole organism level
source: In this light, downstream effects of GCs can be interpreted as evolved responses to MR fluctuations, reallocating resources in the face of shifting demands on the whole organism level.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the meta-analysis findings and evolutionary reasoning.

claim: The residual heterogeneity of the final model did not deviate from a level expected due to sampling variance
source: However, the residual heterogeneity of our final model did not deviate from a level expected due to sampling variance, providing additional support for our third prediction.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the meta-analysis, supporting the conclusion about treatment independence.

claim: Receptor types differ in sensitivity to GCs
source: This is not to say that this also applies to the functional consequences of GC-level variation: it is well known that receptor types differ in sensitivity to GCs (Landys et al., 2006; Sapolsky et al., 2000; Romero, 2004), thereby potentially generating step functions in the response to an increase in GC levels.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established works on GC receptor biology.

claim: The association between MR and GCs is expected to be less evident in a more natural context
source: We restricted the meta-analysis to experimental studies and expect the association between MR and GCs to be less evident in a more natural context.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the authors' reasoning about the differences between experimental and natural conditions.

claim: Associations between GCs and MR will be most evident when animals are maintained at different but stable levels of MR
source: Associations between GCs and MR will be most evident when animals are maintained at different but stable levels of MR because then the rate at which tissues are fuelled is likely to be in equilibrium with the metabolic needs.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the authors' reasoning about equilibrium conditions.

claim: When MR fluctuates, GC variation will track MR fluctuations, but with a time lag
source: When MR fluctuates, for example, due to short-term variation in activity, GC variation will track MR fluctuations, but with a time lag (Box 1), thus adding complexity to the MR/GC association and its detectability.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the authors' reasoning about temporal dynamics, referenced to Box 1.

claim: Experiments yield estimates of associations within the average individual in the study, while data collected in a natural context usually rely on variation between individuals
source: Furthermore, experiments yield estimates of associations within the average individual in the study, while data collected in a natural context usually rely on variation between individuals (but see Malkoc et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a statement about methodological differences between experimental and observational studies.

claim: Associations between individuals will be less strong than the associations within individuals due to individual variation in GC levels and GC reactivity
source: Associations between individuals will be less strong than the associations within individuals due to individual variation in GC levels and GC reactivity (e.g. Liu et al., 1997; Weaver et al., 2004; Yehuda et al., 2014; Taff et al., 2018; Taff et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a prediction supported by citations to studies showing individual variation in GC levels and reactivity.

claim: A strong positive MR/GC correlation was reported for mammals
source: While a strong positive MR/GC correlation was reported for mammals (Haase et al., 2016), Francis et al., 2018 found no consistent GC/MR association in birds and other tetrapod taxa.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Haase et al., 2016.

claim: Francis et al., 2018 found no consistent GC/MR association in birds and other tetrapod taxa
source: While a strong positive MR/GC correlation was reported for mammals (Haase et al., 2016), Francis et al., 2018 found no consistent GC/MR association in birds and other tetrapod taxa.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Francis et al., 2018.

claim: Avian GC variation is positively correlated with estimated thermoregulatory costs
source: However, recent comparative analyses showed avian GC variation to be positively correlated with estimated thermoregulatory costs (Rubalcaba and Jimeno, 2022a), and GC variation in lizards to be positively correlated with body temperature, which directly influences MR in ectotherms (Rubalcaba and Jimeno, 2022b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rubalcaba and Jimeno, 2022a.

claim: GC variation in lizards is positively correlated with body temperature, which directly influences MR in ectotherms
source: However, recent comparative analyses showed avian GC variation to be positively correlated with estimated thermoregulatory costs (Rubalcaba and Jimeno, 2022a), and GC variation in lizards to be positively correlated with body temperature, which directly influences MR in ectotherms (Rubalcaba and Jimeno, 2022b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rubalcaba and Jimeno, 2022b.

claim: The early morning GC increase in humans, known as the 'cortisol awakening response', can be interpreted as preparation for an increase in MR
source: For example, the early morning GC increase in humans, known as the 'cortisol awakening response' (Fries et al., 2009), can be interpreted as preparation for an increase in MR – indeed, human 'early birds' show higher GC levels than 'night owls' in the hour after awakening (Kudielka et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to studies on the cortisol awakening response.

claim: Human 'early birds' show higher GC levels than 'night owls' in the hour after awakening
source: For example, the early morning GC increase in humans, known as the 'cortisol awakening response' (Fries et al., 2009), can be interpreted as preparation for an increase in MR – indeed, human 'early birds' show higher GC levels than 'night owls' in the hour after awakening (Kudielka et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kudielka et al., 2006.

claim: GC levels increase in athletes preceding competition
source: Likewise, GC levels increase in athletes preceding competition (van Paridon et al., 2017), although separating effects of psychological stress from anticipated metabolic needs is difficult in this context.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to van Paridon et al., 2017.

claim: A causal link between MR and GCs is the most parsimonious explanation of the findings
source: We conclude, therefore, that while a causal link between MR and GCs is not the only possible explanation of our findings, we argue it to be the most parsimonious explanation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the meta-analysis results and reasoning about alternative explanations.

claim: Thyroid hormones have been shown to affect MR
source: Direct manipulations of MR could confirm or reject this explanation and may, for example, be achieved using thyroid hormones, which have been shown to affect MR (Moreno et al., 2002; Kim, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing effects of thyroid hormones on MR.

claim: When the function of GCs is to facilitate a level of MR, as opposed to regulate variation in MR, GC administration is not anticipated to induce an increase in MR
source: However, while many studies show that GC administration induces a cascade of effects, when the function of GCs is to facilitate a level of MR, as opposed to regulate variation in MR, we do not anticipate such manipulations to induce an increase in MR (Box 1).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the authors' framework about GC function.

claim: A positive association between GCs and reproductive success may indicate that individuals who are able to sustain high MRs attain higher fitness
source: For example, a positive association between GCs and reproductive success may indicate that individuals who are able to sustain high MRs attain higher fitness (e.g. Bauch et al., 2016), while a negative association indicates the opposite effect (e.g. Ouyang et al., 2013; see Atema et al., 2022, for a more general discussion of this specific contrast).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to studies showing positive GC-fitness associations.

claim: A negative association between GCs and reproductive success indicates that individuals who sustain high MRs attain lower fitness
source: For example, a positive association between GCs and reproductive success may indicate that individuals who are able to sustain high MRs attain higher fitness (e.g. Bauch et al., 2016), while a negative association indicates the opposite effect (e.g. Ouyang et al., 2013; see Atema et al., 2022, for a more general discussion of this specific contrast).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to studies showing negative GC-fitness associations.

claim: GCs suppress immune function
source: Given that GCs have many other downstream effects (Sapolsky et al., 2000), for example, suppressing immune function (Cain and Cidlowski, 2017), and growth (Allen, 1996), this may seem an overly simplistic approach.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cain and Cidlowski, 2017.

claim: GCs suppress growth
source: Given that GCs have many other downstream effects (Sapolsky et al., 2000), for example, suppressing immune function (Cain and Cidlowski, 2017), and growth (Allen, 1996), this may seem an overly simplistic approach.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Allen, 1996.

claim: Downstream effects of GCs may be understood as responses to a system-level readout of the current level of energy metabolism
source: However, in this framework, downstream effects of GCs may be understood as responses to a system-level readout of the current level of energy metabolism, with high levels affecting the allocation of energy to different energy demanding processes.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the authors' framework about GC function.

claim: The link between GCs and energy-demanding processes is asymmetric, in the sense that GCs affect energy allocation to processes like growth, but there is no direct feedback from growth to GC levels
source: In this view, the link between GCs and energy-demanding processes is asymmetric, in the sense that GCs affect energy allocation to, for example, growth, but there is no direct feedback from growth to GC levels.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the authors' framework about GC function.

claim: Heart rate and MR are strongly correlated
source: Among these, we also included those studies reporting heart rate as a metabolic measure as heart rate and MR are strongly correlated (Bevan et al., 1994; Bevan et al., 1995; Butler et al., 2004; Word et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies showing the correlation between heart rate and MR.

claim: The meta-analysis included a total of 21 papers
source: Thus, we included a total of 21 papers (Supplementary file 2) in our analyses, of which 12 were on birds and 9 on mammals.
evidence: This is a direct report of the number of studies included in the meta-analysis.

claim: 12 of the 21 papers included in the meta-analysis were on birds
source: Thus, we included a total of 21 papers (Supplementary file 2) in our analyses, of which 12 were on birds and 9 on mammals.
evidence: This is a direct report of the taxonomic distribution of studies in the meta-analysis.

claim: 9 of the 21 papers included in the meta-analysis were on mammals
source: Thus, we included a total of 21 papers (Supplementary file 2) in our analyses, of which 12 were on birds and 9 on mammals.
evidence: This is a direct report of the taxonomic distribution of studies in the meta-analysis.

claim: 9 of the 22 papers included more than one experimental treatment, yielding a total of 35 effect sizes
source: Also, 9 of the 22 papers included more than one experimental treatment, yielding a total of 35 effect sizes.
evidence: This is a direct report of the number of effect sizes included in the meta-analysis.
